appraisal_events.evidence: Swann rants that the Verdurins' circle is "le dernier cercle de Dante" and "une mégère comme la Verdurin," praising the faubourg Saint-Germain's wisdom in refusing to know such people.
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann's jealous tirade continues to savage the Verdurins, but the passage frames it as his own inflated, self-serving rage rather than a narrator-endorsed judgment.

appraisal_events.evidence: The narrator states Swann's own voice was more clear-sighted than he was, choosing its disgusted words "pour assouvir sa colère que pour exprimer sa pensée"; moments later Swann rushes back out, having found a way to get himself invited to the Chatou dinner he had just denounced.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator exposes Swann's grand renunciation of the Verdurin milieu as hollow performance, immediately betrayed by his real, urgent wish to be included after all.

appraisal_events.evidence: When Cottard asks whether they will see M. Swann, Mme Verdurin exclaims "j'espère bien que non! ... il est assommant, bête et mal élevé"; Cottard instantly retreats into abashed, wordless laughter, and "il ne fut plus question de Swann chez les Verdurin."
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Verdurin publicly denounces Swann and Cottard's immediate capitulation confirms it: Swann is decisively cast out of the little clan's conversation and society.

status_effects.explanation: Swann's continued jealous denunciation brands her a shrew and worse, though this is his ironized private rage rather than an endorsed verdict.
Cottard's total, comic capitulation to her verdict on Swann shows her authority over the little clan going unchallenged and immediately obeyed.
The narrator reveals that Swann's lofty condemnation of the Verdurins was insincere, and he is immediately shown scheming to get back into their good graces.
In a separate, later scene, Mme Verdurin bluntly calls him boring, stupid, and ill-mannered in front of Cottard, a sharp public verdict against him.
Swann is decisively barred from the Verdurin circle: his failed scheme to get invited fails outright, and afterward he is not even mentioned in their conversation.
Cottard's abrupt capitulation into abashed, wordless laughter reads as a small comic diminishment, showing him utterly unable to hold his own view against Mme Verdurin's verdict.

ambiguities: Swann's denunciation of the Verdurins (E1) is his own ironized jealous rage, so the negative effect on Mme Verdurin's general appraisal is recorded with lower confidence than the narrator-endorsed events.
